fuentes/riqueza-de-las-naciones/titulo.texto: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

fuentes/riqueza-de-las-naciones/resumen.texto: Explains a country's wealth by the productivity of labor, which grows with the division of labor and the extent of the market. It argues that each individual, in pursuing their own interest, is led “by an invisible hand” to promote the common good, and it criticizes the mercantile system, monopolies and barriers to trade. It assigns the state defense, justice and certain public works.

fuentes/riqueza-de-las-naciones/por_que_.texto: It is the founding work of classical political economy and the enduring reference for advocates of the free market, although its interpreters debate how much room Smith gave to public action.

fuentes/riqueza-de-las-naciones/leer.0.t.texto: Original English text at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/teoria-de-los-sentimientos-moral.texto: Grounds morality in sympathy, the capacity to put oneself in another's place, and in the judgment of an “impartial spectator” that each person learns to carry within. It argues that virtue is formed in social life and not only through reason or interest.
It shows that the author of “The Wealth of Nations” did not reduce human conduct to self-interest; the so-called “Adam Smith problem” debates how the two books can be reconciled.
Original English text at the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/principios-de-economia-politica-.texto: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation

Analyzes how output is divided among landowners, capitalists and workers, with a labor theory of value and a theory of the differential rent of land. It sets out comparative advantage with the example of Portuguese wine and English cloth: two countries gain from trade even if one is more efficient at everything.
Comparative advantage remains the central argument for free trade, and his theory of value was Marx's starting point.
Original English text at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/tratado-de-economia-politica-say.texto: Systematically organizes and popularizes Adam Smith's ideas, dividing economics into production, distribution and consumption. It highlights the role of the entrepreneur and formulates the “law of markets”: products are paid for with products, so there can be no lasting general overproduction.
It was the most widely read economics textbook in Europe and the Americas for decades; “Say's law” was the main target of Keynes's critique.
19th-century English translation at the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/la-ley-bastiat/resumen.texto: Argues that the law exists to protect person, liberty and property, which precede it, and denounces “legal plunder”: the use of the law to take from some what belongs to them and give it to others. He wrote it against the socialism and protectionism of the French Second Republic, a few months before his death.

fuentes/la-ley-bastiat/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the most widely circulated liberal texts and a constant reference for contemporary libertarianism.

fuentes/lo-que-se-ve-y-lo-que-no-se-ve/t.texto: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen

fuentes/lo-que-se-ve-y-lo-que-no-se-ve/r.texto: Argues that the good economist looks not only at the visible effect of a measure but also at the effects that are not seen. With the parable of the broken window it shows that destroying wealth does not create it: the money paid to the glazier is no longer spent on something else.

fuentes/lo-que-se-ve-y-lo-que-no-se-ve/p.texto: The “broken window fallacy” is one of the most common arguments against public spending as an engine of the economy; Hazlitt built “Economics in One Lesson” on it.

fuentes/lo-que-se-ve-y-lo-que-no-se-ve/l.texto: Selected essays of Bastiat in English (including this one and “The Law”) at the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/sobre-la-libertad/resumen.texto: Formulates the “harm principle”: society may limit an individual's liberty only to prevent harm to others, never for the individual's own good. It defends freedom of thought and expression and warns against the tyranny of the majority and the pressure of opinion.

fuentes/sobre-la-libertad/por_que_import.texto: It is the classic text of political liberalism and of the defense of individual liberty against the state and society.

fuentes/sobre-la-libertad/leer.0.titulo.texto: Original English text at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/el-hombre-contra-el-estado/resum.texto: Collects four essays that accuse British liberalism of having become interventionist and foretell a “coming slavery” if the state keeps expanding its functions. It criticizes social legislation and holds that the function of the state is only to protect rights.

fuentes/el-hombre-contra-el-estado/por_q.texto: It is a classic of 19th-century anti-statist individualism, widely cited by 20th-century libertarians.

fuentes/el-hombre-contra-el-estado/leer..texto: English text at the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/la-produccion-de-seguridad/resum.texto: Article in the Journal des économistes that applies the logic of competition to security: if monopoly is harmful in any industry, it is also harmful in the protection of persons and property. It proposes that private companies compete to provide defense and justice.

fuentes/la-produccion-de-seguridad/por_q.texto: It is considered the first statement of what Rothbard called anarcho-capitalism.

fuentes/la-produccion-de-seguridad/leer..texto: English translation published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/sin-traicion/resumen.texto: Series of pamphlets written after the Civil War that deny the authority of the United States Constitution: a contract binds only those who sign it, and no one living signed it. It concludes that government rests not on consent but on force.

fuentes/sin-traicion/por_que_importa.texto: It is a cult text of individualist anarchism and American libertarianism.

fuentes/teoria-de-la-economia-politica-j.texto: Argues that value depends entirely on utility and explains exchange by the “final degree of utility”, the utility of the last unit consumed. It proposes treating economics with mathematical tools, as a calculus of pleasure and pain.
Together with Menger's “Principles” and Walras's “Elements”, it launched the marginalist revolution, which displaced the labor theory of value.
Original English text at the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/elementos-de-economia-pura/resum.texto: Presents the economy as a system of simultaneous equations in which the prices of all goods and services are determined at once, through the trial and error of an imaginary auctioneer. It uses marginal utility (“rareté”) as the basis of demand.

fuentes/elementos-de-economia-pura/por_q.texto: It is the origin of general equilibrium theory, the core of 20th-century mathematical economics.

fuentes/principios-de-economia-marshall/.texto: Combines the classical tradition with marginal analysis through supply and demand curves, the partial equilibrium of each market, elasticity and the distinction between the short and the long run. Written to be accessible, it leaves the mathematics to notes and appendices.
It was the dominant economics textbook in English for forty years and shaped the Cambridge school from which Keynes emerged.
Original English text at the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/bases-alberdi/titulo.texto: Bases and Starting Points for the Political Organization of the Argentine Republic

fuentes/bases-alberdi/resumen.texto: Written in Valparaíso after the fall of Rosas, it proposes a draft constitution for Argentina. It holds that “to govern is to populate” and that the country must attract European immigrants, capital and railways and guarantee property and freedom of trade and industry.

fuentes/bases-alberdi/por_que_importa.texto: It was the main source of the Constitution of 1853, and Argentine liberalism claims it as its founding text.

fuentes/sistema-economico-y-rentistico/t.texto: Economic and Revenue System of the Argentine Confederation According to Its Constitution of 1853

fuentes/sistema-economico-y-rentistico/r.texto: Comments on the Constitution of 1853 from an economic standpoint: it holds that the Constitution guarantees freedom of work, trade and industry, as well as property, and that laws and taxes must respect them. It criticizes the colonial legacy of monopolies and regulations with arguments drawn from Smith and Say.

fuentes/sistema-economico-y-rentistico/p.texto: It is the main economic text of 19th-century Argentine liberalism.

fuentes/rerum-novarum/resumen.texto: Encyclical of Pope Leo XIII “on the condition of workers”. It rejects socialism and defends private property, but condemns exploitation, calls for a just wage, accepts that the state may protect workers and supports workers' associations.

fuentes/rerum-novarum/por_que_importa.texto: It inaugurates the social doctrine of the Church, the basis of social Catholicism, Christian democracy and movements such as Peronism that presented themselves as a “third position” between capitalism and communism.

fuentes/rerum-novarum/leer.0.titulo.texto: Spanish text on the Holy See website

fuentes/principios-de-economia-menger/re.texto: Explains the value of goods by the importance people attribute to them for satisfying their needs, and not by the labor embodied in them. It orders goods by their distance from consumption and explains the spontaneous origin of money as the most saleable good.

fuentes/principios-de-economia-menger/po.texto: It is the founding work of the Austrian school and one of the three texts of the marginalist revolution.

fuentes/principios-de-economia-menger/le.texto: English translation published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/investigaciones-sobre-el-metodo/.texto: Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences with Special Reference to Economics

Defends abstract economic theory and methodological individualism against Gustav Schmoller's German historical school, which favored historical description. It argues that many social institutions, such as money or law, arise as the unintended result of individual actions.
It sparked the Methodenstreit, the dispute over method that gave the Austrian school its name and identity.
English translation published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/capital-e-interes/resumen.texto: The first volume reviews and criticizes earlier theories of interest, including Marx's exploitation theory; the second, the “Positive Theory of Capital” (1889), explains interest by the preference for present over future goods and by the greater productivity of indirect or “roundabout” methods of production.

fuentes/capital-e-interes/por_que_import.texto: It is the basis of the Austrian theory of capital and of the business cycle, taken up by Mises and Hayek.

fuentes/capital-e-interes/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by William Smart (1890) at the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/la-conclusion-del-sistema-marxia.texto: Karl Marx and the Close of His System

Examines the third volume of “Capital”, published by Engels in 1894, and argues that it contradicts the first: if prices of production depart from labor values, Marx's theory of value does not explain actual prices. This is the so-called “transformation problem”.
It is the classic liberal critique of Marx's economics; Rudolf Hilferding replied to it from a Marxist standpoint.

fuentes/teoria-del-dinero-y-del-credito/.texto: The Theory of Money and Credit

Applies marginal utility to money and explains its value with the “regression theorem”, which traces it back to its origin as a commodity. It argues that the expansion of bank credit without savings to back it artificially lowers interest rates, causes erroneous investments and ends in crisis.
It contains the seed of the Austrian business cycle theory, which Hayek developed in the 1930s.
English translation published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/calculo-economico-socialismo/tit.texto: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth

fuentes/calculo-economico-socialismo/res.texto: Argues that without private ownership of the means of production there is no market for them and no prices, and that without prices a planner cannot compare the cost of alternative uses of resources. It concludes that socialism is “the abolition of rational economy”.

fuentes/calculo-economico-socialismo/por.texto: It opened the socialist calculation debate, one of the most important in 20th-century economics.

fuentes/socialismo-mises/titulo.texto: Socialism: An Economic and Sociological Analysis

fuentes/socialismo-mises/resumen.texto: Develops in a full treatise the critique of socialist economic calculation and extends it to the various forms of socialism, to interventionism and to the doctrines that support them. It defends private property and the division of labor as the basis of social cooperation.

fuentes/socialismo-mises/por_que_importa.texto: Reading it drew young people such as Hayek away from socialism; Hayek described it as a conversion.

fuentes/socialismo-mises/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/liberalismo-mises/resumen.texto: A brief exposition of the classical liberal program: private property, freedom, peace, democracy as a means of changing governments without violence, free trade and a limited state. It also discusses international politics and the parties of its time.

fuentes/liberalismo-mises/por_que_import.texto: It is Mises's most accessible political synthesis. A passage crediting fascism with having “for the moment saved” European civilization from Bolshevism is cited by his critics; his defenders point out that the same text rejects it as a lasting solution.

fuentes/liberalismo-mises/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/burocracia-mises/resumen.texto: Contrasts business management, guided by profit and loss, with bureaucratic management, which must be governed by regulations because it has no market criterion for measuring results. It argues that the expansion of the state makes all of society bureaucratic.

fuentes/burocracia-mises/por_que_importa.texto: It is an early text of the liberal critique of the administrative state and a forerunner of public choice theory.

fuentes/burocracia-mises/leer.0.titulo.texto: Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/accion-humana/titulo.texto: Human Action: A Treatise on Economics

fuentes/accion-humana/resumen.texto: A general treatise that grounds economics in praxeology: a priori deductions from the axiom that human beings act purposefully. It brings together the theory of value, money, capital, the cycle and economic calculation, and defends the market economy against socialism and interventionism.

fuentes/accion-humana/por_que_importa.texto: It is Mises's major work and the reference text of the Austrian school, especially in its Rothbardian current; its critics reject its apriorist method.

fuentes/accion-humana/leer.0.titulo.texto: Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/mentalidad-anticapitalista/resum.texto: Attributes hostility toward capitalism to the resentment of those who do not succeed in a society where success depends on satisfying consumers, especially among intellectuals, employees and writers.

fuentes/mentalidad-anticapitalista/por_q.texto: It is a short essay by Mises widely circulated in popular liberal writing; its critics see it as a psychological rather than an economic argument.

fuentes/mentalidad-anticapitalista/leer..texto: Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/seis-lecciones-mises/titulo.texto: Economic Policy: Thoughts for Today and Tomorrow (Six Lessons on Capitalism)

fuentes/seis-lecciones-mises/resumen.texto: The six lectures Mises gave in English at the Universidad de Buenos Aires in 1959, at the invitation of Alberto Benegas Lynch, on capitalism, socialism, interventionism, inflation, foreign investment and ideas. His widow, Margit von Mises, published them in 1979.

fuentes/seis-lecciones-mises/por_que_imp.texto: They mark the arrival of the Austrian school in Argentina and are its most widely read popular text in the country.

fuentes/seis-lecciones-mises/leer.0.titu.texto: Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/precios-y-produccion/resumen.texto: Four lectures given at the London School of Economics that develop the Austrian theory of the cycle: cheap credit alters relative prices and artificially lengthens the structure of production, represented by “Hayekian triangles”, until the lack of real savings forces the crisis.

fuentes/precios-y-produccion/por_que_imp.texto: It was the theoretical basis of Hayek's position in his debate with Keynes and made him known in the English-speaking world.

fuentes/camino-de-servidumbre/resumen.texto: Argues that centralized economic planning, even with good democratic intentions, requires concentrating power and leads to totalitarianism, and that Nazism and communism share that root. It defends the rule of law and competition, though it accepts a minimal social safety net.

fuentes/camino-de-servidumbre/por_que_im.texto: It was a mass success, especially in the condensed Reader's Digest version (1945), and made Hayek a public figure of liberalism.

fuentes/uso-del-conocimiento-en-la-socie.texto: The Use of Knowledge in Society

Article in the American Economic Review arguing that the central economic problem is not allocating given resources but making use of knowledge dispersed among millions of people, which no one possesses in full. The price system works as a communication mechanism that transmits that knowledge.
It is one of the most cited articles in economics and Hayek's strongest argument in the socialist calculation debate.
Original English text at the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/los-fundamentos-de-la-libertad/r.texto: A treatise of political philosophy that defines liberty as the absence of coercion and justifies it by each person's inevitable ignorance: only liberty makes it possible to use dispersed knowledge. It examines the rule of law and criticizes the welfare state, union power and progressive taxation; it closes with the essay “Why I Am Not a Conservative”.

fuentes/los-fundamentos-de-la-libertad/p.texto: It is the most systematic exposition of Hayek's liberalism; according to a widely told anecdote, Margaret Thatcher slammed it down on a table saying “this is what we believe”.

fuentes/derecho-legislacion-y-libertad/r.texto: A three-volume work that distinguishes spontaneous order (“cosmos”) from made order (“taxis”), and law that arises from practice from deliberate legislation. It criticizes “social justice” as a mirage and proposes a constitutional model with a legislative assembly separate from the governmental one.

fuentes/derecho-legislacion-y-libertad/p.texto: It completes Hayek's political philosophy and his critique of unlimited democracy.

fuentes/la-desnacionalizacion-del-dinero.texto: Institute of Economic Affairs pamphlet that proposes abolishing the state monopoly on issuing money and allowing private banks to issue currencies that compete with one another, on the idea that competition would reward the most stable ones and put an end to inflation.
It is the theoretical reference for free banking and currency competition, and was later invoked by advocates of cryptocurrencies.
Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/la-fatal-arrogancia/titulo.texto: The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism

fuentes/la-fatal-arrogancia/resumen.texto: Hayek's last book, edited by William W. Bartley III. It argues that the morality of property, contract and trade arose through cultural evolution rather than design, and that socialism is an intellectual error: the “fatal conceit” of believing that reason can redesign society.

fuentes/la-fatal-arrogancia/por_que_impo.texto: It closes Hayek's body of work with his theory of cultural evolution; how much of the final text is owed to Bartley is debated.

fuentes/sobre-la-teoria-economica-del-so.texto: On the Economic Theory of Socialism

Two-part article in the Review of Economic Studies that replies to Mises: a central planning board can set the prices of the means of production by trial and error, raising them where there is scarcity and lowering them where there is surplus, like Walras's auctioneer. It concludes that “market socialism” can be as efficient as competition.
It is the most cited socialist response in the calculation debate; the Austrians replied that it ignores the knowledge problem and the entrepreneurial function.

fuentes/el-hombre-la-economia-y-el-estad.texto: Treatise that reconstructs the whole of economic theory, from exchange to capital, money and the cycle, on the basis of Mises's praxeology. The part on state intervention, cut by the publisher, was published separately in 1970 as “Power and Market”.
It is the main Austrian treatise after “Human Action” and the economic foundation of Rothbard's anarcho-capitalism.
Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/la-gran-depresion-rothbard/resum.texto: Applies the Austrian theory of the business cycle to the crisis of 1929: it attributes the boom of the 1920s to the Federal Reserve's credit expansion and the depth of the depression to Hoover's interventions, which prevented prices and wages from readjusting.

fuentes/la-gran-depresion-rothbard/por_q.texto: It is the canonical Austrian interpretation of the Great Depression, opposed to the Keynesian one and to the monetarist one of Friedman and Schwartz.

fuentes/la-gran-depresion-rothbard/leer..texto: Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/anatomia-del-estado/resumen.texto: Short essay that defines the State as the organization that obtains its revenue by coercion, through taxes, and claims a monopoly on force in a territory. It analyzes how it legitimizes itself with the support of intellectuals and how it frees itself from constitutional limits.

fuentes/anatomia-del-estado/por_que_impo.texto: It sums up in a few pages the anarcho-capitalist theory of the State.

fuentes/anatomia-del-estado/leer.0.titul.texto: Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/por-una-nueva-libertad/titulo.texto: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto

fuentes/por-una-nueva-libertad/resumen.texto: Sets out the libertarian program on the basis of the “non-aggression axiom”: no one may initiate the use of force against another person or their property. It proposes privatizing streets, education, police, courts and defense, abolishing taxes and dismantling the State.

fuentes/por-una-nueva-libertad/por_que_i.texto: It was the manifesto of the American libertarian movement during its period of growth, shortly after the founding of the Libertarian Party.

fuentes/por-una-nueva-libertad/leer.0.ti.texto: Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/la-etica-de-la-libertad/resumen.texto: Grounds libertarianism in natural law, self-ownership and the original appropriation of unowned resources. From these it derives a theory of punishment, of contract and of children's rights, and it criticizes other liberals such as Hayek, Isaiah Berlin and Nozick.

fuentes/la-etica-de-la-libertad/por_que_.texto: It is the most complete philosophical exposition of Rothbardian anarcho-capitalism; its theses on children's rights are among the most debated.

fuentes/la-etica-de-la-libertad/leer.0.t.texto: Original English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/competencia-y-funcion-empresaria.texto: Criticizes equilibrium theory for leaving out the market process and places at its center the entrepreneur, whose function is to be alert to profit opportunities that others have missed. Competition is a discovery process that corrects errors and coordinates plans.
It is the central work of the modern Austrian school on entrepreneurship.

fuentes/democracia-el-dios-que-fracaso/r.texto: Argues that hereditary monarchy, as private ownership of government, encourages a long-term outlook, whereas democracy, as temporary public ownership, encourages rulers to exploit the country while they last. It proposes a natural order of private property with security provided competitively, and defends restrictions on immigration.

fuentes/democracia-el-dios-que-fracaso/p.texto: It is Hoppe's most influential work on the libertarian right; his critics consider it antidemocratic and exclusionary.

fuentes/dinero-credito-bancario-y-ciclos.texto: Money, Bank Credit, and Economic Cycles

Studies the legal history of the irregular deposit contract since Roman law and argues that fractional-reserve banking is a misappropriation that allows credit to be created without prior saving. Using the Austrian theory of the business cycle, it explains crises by that expansion, and proposes a 100% reserve requirement and free banking.
It is Huerta de Soto's best-known work, translated into numerous languages, and a reference of the Austrian school in the Spanish-speaking world.

fuentes/consecuencias-economicas-de-la-p.texto: The Economic Consequences of the Peace

Written after resigning from the British delegation to the Paris Peace Conference, it criticizes the Treaty of Versailles for imposing on Germany reparations impossible to pay, which would ruin its economy and that of Europe. It portrays Clemenceau, Wilson and Lloyd George harshly, and proposes reducing reparations and canceling war debts.
It made Keynes famous and fixed for decades the idea of a “Carthaginian peace”; later historians debate whether he exaggerated the burden of the reparations.
Original English text at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/breve-tratado-reforma-monetaria/.texto: Analyzes postwar inflation and deflation and their effects on creditors, debtors and workers, and proposes that central banks pursue domestic price stability instead of returning to the gold standard at the prewar parity. It contains the phrase “in the long run we are all dead”.
It shows the early Keynes as a monetary theorist and a critic of the return to gold that Britain carried out in 1925.

fuentes/el-final-del-laissez-faire/resum.texto: Argues that laissez-faire cannot be deduced from the principles of economics and that private and social interest do not always coincide. It proposes that the State take on what no one else does, such as controlling credit, directing saving and investment and producing information, without abandoning private enterprise.

fuentes/el-final-del-laissez-faire/por_q.texto: It is the manifesto of Keynes's “new liberalism”, halfway between the free market and socialism.

fuentes/posibilidades-economicas-de-nues.texto: In the midst of the Depression, Keynes predicts that within a hundred years technical progress and capital accumulation will raise living standards four to eight times and solve the “economic problem”, so that working some fifteen hours a week would be enough. The challenge will then be knowing how to use leisure.
His growth forecast largely came true in much of the rich world, while that of the short working week did not; it is a key text in debates on work and automation.
Original English text on the Yale University website

fuentes/teoria-general-keynes/titulo.texto: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money

fuentes/teoria-general-keynes/resumen.texto: Argues that a market economy can become stuck with involuntary unemployment because the level of employment depends on effective demand, and that investment, driven by uncertain expectations and “animal spirits”, does not adjust to saving on its own. It introduces the propensity to consume, the multiplier and liquidity preference, and justifies the State sustaining demand.

fuentes/teoria-general-keynes/por_que_im.texto: It founded modern macroeconomics and guided Western economic policy until the 1970s; its Austrian and monetarist critics blame it for the expansion of public spending and postwar inflation.

fuentes/keynes-y-los-clasicos/titulo.texto: Mr. Keynes and the “Classics”: A Suggested Interpretation

fuentes/keynes-y-los-clasicos/resumen.texto: Econometrica article that summarizes the “General Theory” in a system of two curves: one for equilibrium in the goods market (IS) and another for the money market (LM). It presents classical theory as a special case and Keynes's as the one that applies when the interest rate cannot fall any further.

fuentes/keynes-y-los-clasicos/por_que_im.texto: The IS-LM model became the standard way of teaching Keynes and the basis of the neoclassical synthesis; post-Keynesians criticize it for having tamed the original work.

fuentes/economics-samuelson/resumen.texto: University textbook that presented the neoclassical synthesis: Keynesian macroeconomics for employment and price microeconomics for the allocation of resources. It went through nineteen editions, the last ones with William Nordhaus.

fuentes/economics-samuelson/por_que_impo.texto: It was the best-selling economics textbook in the world and trained several generations of students, including in Latin America.

fuentes/informe-beveridge/titulo.texto: Social Insurance and Allied Services (Beveridge Report)

fuentes/informe-beveridge/resumen.texto: Report commissioned by the British government in the middle of the war that proposes a universal system of social insurance funded by contributions, family allowances and a national health service, to defeat the “five giants”: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness.

fuentes/informe-beveridge/por_que_import.texto: It was the basis of the postwar British welfare state, including the National Health Service (1948), and a model for other countries.

fuentes/la-sociedad-opulenta/resumen.texto: Argues that the postwar American economy is still guided by the “conventional wisdom” of scarcity when it is already affluent: advertising creates the wants that production satisfies, while public services are neglected. It proposes investing more in education, infrastructure and public goods.

fuentes/la-sociedad-opulenta/por_que_imp.texto: It popularized the expression “conventional wisdom” and the contrast between private affluence and public squalor.

fuentes/aspectos-politicos-del-pleno-emp.texto: Article in The Political Quarterly arguing that, although governments now know how to achieve full employment through public spending, business leaders will oppose maintaining it because it weakens factory discipline and their political power. It foresees a “political business cycle” of expansions before elections and austerity afterward.
It is a classic text of post-Keynesian and Marxist political economy on the political limits of Keynesianism.
Original English text reproduced by MR Online

fuentes/economia-de-la-competencia-imper.texto: Drops the assumption of perfect competition and analyzes markets with few sellers or differentiated products, in which firms set prices. It introduces monopsony, the power of a single buyer, for example of labor, to push down wages.
Together with Edward Chamberlin's work of the same year, it renewed the theory of markets and of the firm.

fuentes/estabilizando-una-economia-inest.texto: Sets out the financial instability hypothesis: during booms, firms and banks move from prudent financing to speculative and then “Ponzi” financing, which depends on asset prices continuing to rise, until the fragility bursts. It defends a big government and a central bank acting as lender of last resort to prevent depressions.
It was rediscovered after the 2008 financial crisis as an explanation of how stability breeds instability.

fuentes/historia-monetaria-de-estados-un.texto: A Monetary History of the United States, 1867–1960

Written with Anna Schwartz for the National Bureau of Economic Research, it reconstructs the quantity of money in the United States over almost a century and its relationship to prices and output. It argues that the Great Depression was a “great contraction” caused by the Federal Reserve, which let the quantity of money fall by a third.
It is the empirical foundation of monetarism; in 2002 Ben Bernanke, then a governor of the Federal Reserve, acknowledged to Friedman and Schwartz that they were right.

fuentes/capitalismo-y-libertad/resumen.texto: Argues that economic freedom is a condition of political freedom and proposes replacing state interventions with markets: school vouchers, floating exchange rates, an end to occupational licensing and military conscription, and a negative income tax in place of social programs.

fuentes/capitalismo-y-libertad/por_que_i.texto: It is the program of Chicago liberalism for the general public; several of its proposals, such as the volunteer army or school vouchers, were later implemented.

fuentes/la-responsabilidad-social-de-la-.texto: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits

Article in The New York Times Magazine arguing that executives are employees of the shareholders and that spending their money on social ends amounts to levying a tax without a mandate. The only social responsibility of business is to increase its profits within the rules of the game.
It founded the “Friedman doctrine” or shareholder primacy, which dominated corporate management and is the target of proposals for stakeholder capitalism.

fuentes/libertad-de-elegir/resumen.texto: Written with his wife Rose Friedman to accompany a PBS television series, it defends the free market against the welfare state, regulation and inflation, with examples from the United States, Britain, Hong Kong and India.

fuentes/libertad-de-elegir/por_que_impor.texto: It was a bestseller and the series aired in many countries; it accompanied the market turn of Thatcher and Reagan.

fuentes/el-calculo-del-consenso/titulo.texto: The Calculus of Consent: Logical Foundations of Constitutional Democracy

fuentes/el-calculo-del-consenso/resumen.texto: Written with Gordon Tullock, it analyzes collective decisions on the assumption that voters and legislators pursue their own interest, as in the market. It studies vote trading, the cost of majority rules and why a constitution should require larger majorities for certain decisions.

fuentes/el-calculo-del-consenso/por_que_.texto: It is the founding work of public choice theory.

fuentes/el-problema-del-costo-social/res.texto: Argues that harms between neighbors, such as smoke from a factory, are reciprocal problems, and that if bargaining cost nothing the parties would reach the efficient outcome whatever the legal assignment of rights, which later came to be called the “Coase theorem”. Since bargaining does have costs, the law matters.

fuentes/el-problema-del-costo-social/por.texto: It founded the economic analysis of law and is one of the most cited articles in economics.

fuentes/la-economia-en-una-leccion/resum.texto: Popular work that sums up economics in a single lesson: look at the long-term effects of each policy on all groups, not just on one in the short run. It applies Bastiat's broken window fallacy to public works, tariffs, price controls, the minimum wage and inflation.

fuentes/la-economia-en-una-leccion/por_q.texto: It is one of the best-selling economics books and a classic gateway to economic liberalism.

fuentes/la-economia-en-una-leccion/leer..texto: Free digital edition from the Foundation for Economic Education

fuentes/yo-el-lapiz/resumen.texto: A pencil tells its story: the wood, the graphite, the eraser and the lacquer come from thousands of people in different countries who do not know one another and whom no one coordinates, and none of whom would know how to make it alone. It thus illustrates the spontaneous order of the market.

fuentes/yo-el-lapiz/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the most widely circulated popular essays of liberalism, popularized by Milton Friedman in “Free to Choose”.

fuentes/yo-el-lapiz/leer.0.titulo.texto: Free digital edition from the Foundation for Economic Education

fuentes/declaracion-de-propositos-mont-p.texto: Statement of Aims of the Mont Pelerin Society

Text adopted when the society was founded, in April 1947. It warns that the central values of civilization are in danger from the spread of arbitrary power and the loss of faith in private property and the competitive market, and proposes studying the rule of law, the redefinition of the functions of the State and the international order.
It is the founding document of the international network of postwar neoliberalism.
Text on the Mont Pelerin Society website

fuentes/el-ladrillo/titulo.texto: El ladrillo: Foundations of the Economic Policy of the Chilean Military Government

fuentes/el-ladrillo/resumen.texto: Economic program drafted in 1972 and 1973 by Chilean economists, most of them trained at the University of Chicago, which circulated in mimeographed copies so bulky that they earned it its nickname (“the brick”). It proposed trade liberalization, price deregulation, privatizations and deficit reduction, and was handed to the Military Junta after the 1973 coup.

fuentes/el-ladrillo/por_que_importa.texto: It was the basis of the market reforms of the Pinochet dictatorship, which its supporters call the “miracle of Chile” and its critics associate with repression and rising inequality.

fuentes/el-ladrillo/leer.0.titulo.texto: Edition by the Centro de Estudios Públicos of Chile

fuentes/lo-que-washington-entiende-por-r.texto: What Washington Means by Policy Reform

Paper for a conference of the Institute for International Economics in November 1989. It lists ten reforms on which, according to the author, the Washington-based institutions agreed: fiscal discipline, reordering of public spending, tax reform, market-determined interest rates, a competitive exchange rate, trade liberalization, foreign investment, privatization, deregulation and property rights.
It gave its name to the “Washington Consensus”, a byword for the reforms of the 1990s in Latin America.
Text on the Peterson Institute for International Economics website

fuentes/el-manantial/resumen.texto: Novel about Howard Roark, an architect who refuses to adapt his designs to other people's taste and prefers failure to compromise. It sets the creative individual against those who live by the opinion of others.

fuentes/el-manantial/por_que_importa.texto: It was Rand's first major success and the literary presentation of her individualism; it was adapted for film in 1949.

fuentes/la-rebelion-de-atlas/resumen.texto: Novel in which the most productive businesspeople, inventors and artists of a declining United States, summoned by John Galt, go on strike against a State that regulates and plunders them, and the country collapses without them. It includes a long speech setting out the Objectivist philosophy.

fuentes/la-rebelion-de-atlas/por_que_imp.texto: It is Rand's most influential work and a touchstone of libertarianism and the pro-market right; her critics consider it an apology for selfishness and inequality.

fuentes/la-virtud-del-egoismo/resumen.texto: Collects essays by Rand and Nathaniel Branden that set out Objectivist ethics: rational self-interest as the moral standard, the rejection of altruism as a duty and the defense of individual rights and of capitalism as the only moral system.

fuentes/la-virtud-del-egoismo/por_que_im.texto: It is the most direct exposition of Rand's ethics.

fuentes/anarquia-estado-y-utopia/resumen.texto: Argues that a minimal State, limited to protection against force, theft and fraud, can arise legitimately from anarchy without violating rights, and that any more extensive State violates them. With his entitlement theory of justice and the example of the basketball player Wilt Chamberlain, he responds to Rawls's distributive justice.

fuentes/anarquia-estado-y-utopia/por_que.texto: It is the most important academic work of libertarianism and the main reply to “A Theory of Justice”.

fuentes/la-maquinaria-de-la-libertad/tit.texto: The Machinery of Freedom: Guide to a Radical Capitalism

fuentes/la-maquinaria-de-la-libertad/res.texto: Defends a stateless “radical capitalism” with arguments from efficiency rather than natural rights: it describes how private protection agencies and competing courts could provide law and security, and discusses examples such as medieval Iceland.

fuentes/la-maquinaria-de-la-libertad/por.texto: Along with Rothbard's books, it is a founding text of anarcho-capitalism, in its consequentialist variant.

fuentes/la-maquinaria-de-la-libertad/lee.texto: Digital edition on the author's website

fuentes/teoria-del-desenvolvimiento-econ.texto: Distinguishes the “circular flow” of a stationary economy from development, which occurs when innovating entrepreneurs introduce new combinations: products, methods, markets, raw materials or organizations. Bank credit finances these innovations and entrepreneurial profit rewards them until imitation dissolves it.
It placed innovation and the entrepreneur at the center of the theory of growth.

fuentes/capitalismo-socialismo-y-democra.texto: Describes capitalism as a process of “creative destruction” in which innovations sweep away old firms and techniques. It predicts that it will be replaced by socialism not because of its failures but because of its successes, which bureaucratize innovation and create hostile intellectuals, and it defines democracy as a competition among elites for votes.
It popularized the expression “creative destruction”, and its elitist theory of democracy influenced political science.

fuentes/la-gran-transformacion/resumen.texto: Argues that the self-regulating market economy of the 19th century was a deliberate creation of the state and that, by treating labor, land and money as commodities, it threatened to destroy society, which responded with a “double movement” of protection. It attributes the interwar crisis and fascism to that clash.

fuentes/la-gran-transformacion/por_que_i.texto: It is the main historical critique of the economic liberalism of its time, written in parallel with “The Road to Serfdom”, and a reference work of economic sociology.

fuentes/teoria-de-juegos-y-comportamient.texto: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior

Written by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern, it formalizes situations in which the outcome of each decision depends on the decisions of others. It develops the theory of zero-sum games and proposes an axiomatic theory of expected utility.
It founded game theory, which became a central tool of economics, political science and military strategy.

fuentes/equilibrio-de-nash/resumen.texto: One-page note in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences proving that every finite game has at least one equilibrium: a combination of strategies in which no player gains by changing their own if the others do not change theirs. It thus extends game theory to non-cooperative games.

fuentes/equilibrio-de-nash/por_que_impor.texto: The Nash equilibrium is the central concept of modern game theory, with applications ranging from auctions to evolutionary biology.

fuentes/teoria-de-las-perspectivas/titul.texto: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk

fuentes/teoria-de-las-perspectivas/resum.texto: Econometrica article written with Amos Tversky that shows through experiments that people violate expected utility theory: they evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, feel losses more than equivalent gains and misweight probabilities.

fuentes/teoria-de-las-perspectivas/por_q.texto: It is the foundation of behavioral economics and one of the most cited articles in the social sciences.

fuentes/el-capital-en-el-siglo-xxi/resum.texto: Reconstructs from tax data the distribution of income and wealth in rich countries since the 18th century. It argues that when the return on capital exceeds growth (r > g) inherited wealth becomes concentrated, that the lower inequality of the mid-20th century was an exception caused by the wars and public policy, and proposes a global progressive tax on capital.

fuentes/el-capital-en-el-siglo-xxi/por_q.texto: It became a worldwide success after its English translation in 2014 and reopened the debate on inequality; its critics dispute the data and the mechanics of r > g.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-bretton-woods/resume.texto: Final act of the July 1944 conference that created the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. It established a system of fixed but adjustable exchange rates against the dollar, convertible into gold at 35 dollars an ounce, with the IMF as lender in case of balance-of-payments imbalances.

fuentes/acuerdos-de-bretton-woods/por_qu.texto: It organized the postwar international monetary system until 1971 and created the two most influential multilateral financial institutions.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-la-cepal/titulo.texto: The Economic Development of Latin America and Its Principal Problems

fuentes/manifiesto-de-la-cepal/resumen.texto: Study presented to ECLA in 1949 that criticizes the international division of labor: the countries of the periphery that export raw materials suffer a deterioration in their terms of trade against the industrial centers, because the fruits of technical progress remain in the center. It proposes industrialization as a path to development.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-la-cepal/por_que_i.texto: Albert Hirschman called it the ECLA “manifesto”; it founded Latin American structuralism and guided import substitution policy for decades.

fuentes/formacion-economica-del-brasil/r.texto: Economic history of Brazil since colonial times, organized around the export cycles of sugar, gold and coffee. It explains underdevelopment by dependence on primary exports and the concentration of income, and makes the case for industrialization.

fuentes/formacion-economica-del-brasil/p.texto: It is the classic of Brazilian economic history and a model of ECLA's historical-structural method.

fuentes/la-economia-argentina-ferrer/res.texto: Economic history of Argentina divided into stages according to the country's mode of integration into the world economy: the regional subsistence economies, the agro-export expansion and the non-integrated industrialization since 1930. It argues that development requires integrating industry and overcoming the external bottleneck.

fuentes/la-economia-argentina-ferrer/por.texto: It is one of the most widely read economics books in Argentina and a reference work of local structuralist thought; it went through numerous updated editions.

fuentes/dependencia-y-desarrollo/titulo.texto: Dependency and Development in Latin America

fuentes/dependencia-y-desarrollo/resumen.texto: Written with Enzo Faletto at ECLA's Latin American Institute for Economic and Social Planning, it analyzes Latin American development according to each country's class alliances and forms of linkage with the world market. It argues that a “dependent development” associated with foreign capital is possible without overcoming dependency.

fuentes/dependencia-y-desarrollo/por_que.texto: It is the most influential and least deterministic version of dependency theory.

fuentes/el-desarrollo-del-subdesarrollo/.texto: Monthly Review article arguing that Latin America's underdevelopment is not an original state but the result of centuries of subordinate integration into world capitalism, in a chain of metropolises and satellites. It concludes that development requires breaking those ties.
It is the most widely circulated text of the radical version of dependency theory.

fuentes/hay-que-pasar-el-invierno/resume.texto: Address by Frondizi's economy minister, shortly after taking office in June 1959, announcing the continuation of the stabilization plan agreed with the IMF, with wage restraint and public spending cuts, and asking the population for sacrifices with the phrase “hay que pasar el invierno” (“we have to get through the winter”).

fuentes/hay-que-pasar-el-invierno/por_qu.texto: The phrase became an emblem of austerity plans in Argentina.

fuentes/la-noche-del-16-de-enero/resumen.texto: A courtroom play that Rand wrote in 1933, inspired by the death of the Swedish industrialist Ivar Kreuger. In the trial for the murder of the businessman Bjorn Faulkner, his secretary and lover, Karen Andre, is tried; the play does not show the events, and the jury, made up of spectators chosen at random, must decide on the testimony, so the ending depends on its verdict. It premiered in Los Angeles in October 1934 as “Woman on Trial” and moved to Broadway in 1935-1936, where it ran for seven months. Rand argued with the producer Al Woods over the changes, and in 1968 she published a revised version as the “definitive” one.

fuentes/la-noche-del-16-de-enero/por_que.texto: Rand wanted to dramatize the conflict between individualism and conformity: what the jurors decided showed which of the two they preferred. It was her first work produced on stage.

fuentes/los-que-vivimos/resumen.texto: Rand's first novel, which she finished in 1934 and which was rejected by several publishers until Macmillan published it in 1936. It depicts life in Petrograd between 1922 and 1925: Kira Argounova, the daughter of a bourgeois family whose textile factory the Soviet state confiscated, wants to be an engineer and falls in love with Leo Kovalensky; Andrei Taganov, an idealistic communist in the political police (GPU), is her friend and falls in love with her, and Kira becomes his lover to pay for Leo's sanatorium, as Leo is ill with tuberculosis. It shows the queues, the rationing and the state's control over work and study.

fuentes/los-que-vivimos/por_que_importa.texto: It was her first text against communism. Rand, born in St. Petersburg and emigrated in 1926, said in the foreword that it was the closest thing to an autobiography she would write. It sold more than three million copies.

fuentes/himno/soporte.texto: Novella (Cassell, London, 1938; revised edition, United States, 1946)

fuentes/himno/resumen.texto: A dystopian novella written in the summer of 1937 and first published in the United Kingdom in 1938 by Cassell. In a future without a date, humanity has returned to a dark age and the individual has been abolished: people speak in the plural, and each is assigned a trade. Equality 7-2521, assigned to street sweeping, secretly carries out scientific research, flees to a forest with Liberty 5-3000 and recovers the word “I.”

fuentes/himno/por_que_importa.texto: It is the briefest statement of Rand's opposition to collectivism. It was published in the United States only after the success of The Fountainhead, in a text that the author revised in 1946.

fuentes/himno/leer.0.titulo.texto: Project Gutenberg (public domain in the United States)

fuentes/capitalismo-el-ideal-desconocido.texto: A collection of essays, almost all by Rand, with others by Nathaniel Branden, Alan Greenspan and Robert Hessen, that defend laissez-faire capitalism, defined as a complete separation between state and economy, “as between church and state,” on moral grounds and not only economic ones. The first part deals with theory and history, with answers to common objections; the second with issues of the 1960s such as student protests. The essays on the encyclical “Populorum progressio” and on the Vietnam War were added in the 1967 paperback edition.

It applies Objectivism to politics. Rand states that her followers are not “conservatives” but “radicals for capitalism”; Nozick and others argue that grounding individual rights in egoism does not work.

fuentes/principios-de-economia-politica-.texto: A treatise on political economy that was one of the most important textbooks of the mid-19th century. Besides descriptive questions, such as which nations benefit most from trade based on comparative advantage (according to Mill, those whose demand for other countries' goods is more elastic), it addresses normative questions, such as ideal systems of political economy, and criticizes proposals such as communism and socialism.

Together with “A System of Logic,” it consolidated Mill's reputation as a public intellectual. His sympathetic attitude toward the socialism of his time, in particular Fourierism, earned him the esteem of part of the working class, and it was used as a basic textbook at Oxford until 1919.
Full text (Ashley edition, 1909) on the Library of Economics and Liberty
Abridged edition by J. Laurence Laughlin, with notes, on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/el-utilitarismo-mill/soporte.texto: Essay (three articles in Fraser's Magazine in 1861; collected in book form in 1863)

fuentes/el-utilitarismo-mill/resumen.texto: Mill sets out and defends the utilitarianism he received from Jeremy Bentham: happiness is the only thing desired for its own sake, and the aim of ethical life is to maximize it, according to the “principle of utility.” He departs from Bentham in trying for a more refined version, one that gives prominence to intellectual pleasures, personal development and conventional moral rules, and he responds to the criticisms the theory had received.

fuentes/el-utilitarismo-mill/por_que_imp.texto: It was harshly criticized when published; since then it has gained popularity.

fuentes/gobierno-representativo-mill/res.texto: Mill argues that representative government is the ideal form and that the function of parliaments is less to legislate than to serve as a place of public debate on the opinions of the population and to control those who prepare and administer the laws. He defends proportional representation and the single transferable vote, proposed earlier by Thomas Hare, and, at the same time, that better-educated voters should have more votes than less-educated ones, to prevent class legislation by the latter, though without the educated minority being able to legislate for its own benefit.

fuentes/gobierno-representativo-mill/por.texto: It was published in 1861, two years after “On Liberty.”

fuentes/para-el-nuevo-intelectual/soport.texto: Book (Random House; excerpts from novels and an essay)

fuentes/para-el-nuevo-intelectual/resume.texto: Her first full-length book of nonfiction. It gathers speeches from her novels, above all from “The Fountainhead” and “Atlas Shrugged” — among them those on the philosophical nature of money, the condemnation the successful industrialist receives, socialized medicine, the pursuit of profit versus the public good, and a 60-page exposition of Objectivism — plus a central essay, a revision of a lecture at Yale in November 1960, on the history of philosophy. In it Rand calls “Attila” whoever used physical force to achieve his ends, and “sorcerer” whoever, with words, persuaded people to go against their reason, often to the benefit of the Attila of the moment; she sees both as a force of evil in history.

fuentes/para-el-nuevo-intelectual/por_qu.texto: It was the first of several volumes of Rand's essays and speeches, and the last she published with Random House. Sidney Hook, in The New York Times Book Review, called it “a unique combination of tautology and extravagant absurdity.”

fuentes/pensar-rapido-pensar-despacio/re.texto: Kahneman distinguishes two modes of thinking: System 1, fast, instinctive and emotional, and System 2, slower, deliberative and logical. He summarizes decades of research, often done with Amos Tversky — cognitive biases, prospect theory and loss aversion, happiness — and argues that people are overconfident in their judgment. He also distinguishes between the “Econs” of economic theory and real humans, and between the experiencing self and the remembering self.

fuentes/pensar-rapido-pensar-despacio/po.texto: The columnist Jason Zweig helped write and research it. It was a bestseller; the reliability of some of the priming studies it cites was questioned during the replication crisis in psychology.

fuentes/capital-e-ideologia/resumen.texto: Piketty describes it as largely a continuation of “Capital in the Twenty-First Century,” with a broader scope. It explores historical and current justifications for inequality and proposes ways of redistributing wealth, among them an “inheritance for all”: a payment that each country would give its citizens at age 25. According to the passage Paul Krugman quotes, for Piketty inequality is not economic or technological but ideological and political.

fuentes/capital-e-ideologia/por_que_impo.texto: Tyler Cowen criticized him for distrusting the rich rather than the concentrated power of the state, and Raghuram Rajan argued that studies refute the claim that today's rich are mainly rentiers. Piketty refused to censor parts of the book, and for that reason it was not published in mainland China.

fuentes/peticion-de-los-fabricantes-de-v.texto: A satire against protectionism. Candlemakers and makers of other lighting industries ask the Chamber of Deputies of the July Monarchy to protect them from the unfair competition of a foreign power, the Sun, and list the advantages of blocking it out: greater consumption of tallow, vegetable oil, resinous trees and whale oil, and with them more livestock, crops, bees and shipping.
Together with “The Law” and the parable of the broken window, it is one of the works for which Bastiat is best known.
Original French (Œuvres complètes, Guillaumin) on Wikisource
“Economic Sophisms,” English translation on the Library of Economics and Liberty

fuentes/individualismo-y-orden-economico.texto: Essay collection (University of Chicago Press and Routledge)

It gathers essays from the 1930s and 1940s ranging from moral philosophy and the methodology of the social sciences to economic theory, to contrast free markets with planned economies. It includes “Individualism: True and False,” delivered at University College Dublin on December 17, 1945, where he distinguishes a British individualism, which defends an order that arises from law and liberty, from a French one, which leads to expanding the authority of the state and which Hayek calls false; “Economics and Knowledge” (1936), “The Use of Knowledge in Society” and “The Meaning of Competition.”
Many libertarians regard it as a classic; economists such as Elinor Ostrom, James Buchanan and Milton Friedman, all Nobel laureates, cited its arguments.
English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/gobierno-omnipotente-mises/titul.texto: Omnipotent Government: The Rise of the Total State and Total War

fuentes/gobierno-omnipotente-mises/resum.texto: Mises argues that Nazism is a variant of orthodox socialist theory; most historians, by contrast, place Nazism on the far right, as a form of fascism. At the same time he criticizes economic interventionism, central planning of industry, the welfare state and world government, and denounces the Western Allied powers for moving toward the total state.

fuentes/gobierno-omnipotente-mises/por_q.texto: It is Mises's critique of totalitarianism and state socialism, with Nazism as the example. The Mises Institute put it online in 2004.

fuentes/gobierno-omnipotente-mises/leer..texto: English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/teoria-e-historia-mises/titulo.texto: Theory and History: An Interpretation of Social and Economic Evolution

fuentes/teoria-e-historia-mises/resumen.texto: A treatise that continues Mises's social science system and gives more epistemological support to “Human Action.” It develops methodological dualism, the concept of thymology, a historical branch of the sciences of human action, and his critique of Marxist materialism. It holds that determinism, materialism, historicism, scientism, positivism and behaviorism committed epistemological and methodological errors.

fuentes/teoria-e-historia-mises/por_que_.texto: Murray Rothbard considered it one of the most important works of Mises's career, together with “The Theory of Money and Credit,” “Socialism” and “Human Action,” and the most overlooked.

fuentes/teoria-e-historia-mises/leer.0.t.texto: English text published by the Mises Institute

fuentes/fundamentos-del-analisis-economi.texto: Book (Harvard University Press; based on his 1941 doctoral thesis)

Samuelson seeks to show a common mathematical structure underlying several branches of economics, starting from two principles: the maximizing behavior of agents (consumer utility, firm profits) and the stability of equilibrium. He formalizes the method of comparative statics and its “correspondence principle,” according to which the stability of equilibrium implies testable predictions about how it changes when parameters vary.
Among other contributions, it advanced the theory of index numbers and generalized welfare economics. Its cover quotes J. Willard Gibbs's motto: “Mathematics is a language.”

fuentes/valor-y-capital-hicks/titulo.texto: Value and Capital: An Inquiry into Some Fundamental Principles of Economic Theory

fuentes/valor-y-capital-hicks/resumen.texto: Hicks wrote it mainly during his years at Cambridge, building on his earlier work in London. He extends consumer theory using only ordinal utility, without interpersonal comparisons; he separates the effect of a price change into substitution effect and income effect; he carries out a parallel analysis of production; and he extends general equilibrium theory to economic dynamics, distinguishing temporary equilibrium from long-run equilibrium through agents' expectations.

fuentes/valor-y-capital-hicks/por_que_im.texto: It is regarded as a classic exposition of microeconomics, and the distinction between substitution effect and income effect is now standard.

fuentes/la-traicion-de-la-derecha-estado.texto: The Betrayal of the American Right
Book (written in the early 1970s; published by the Mises Institute in 2007)

Rothbard argues that the Old Right of the United States, which existed from the mid-1920s to the mid-1950s, was a libertarian, anti-establishment movement that opposed the New Deal and US intervention abroad, and that it died out in favor of a more interventionist right during the Cold War. According to Rothbard, the New Right, which emerged in the 1960s, embraced the establishment and became more statist and traditionally conservative. The book also describes Rothbard's own intellectual development.

Rothbard points out the irony that the term “establishment,” today used as a reproach by the left, was first applied to the United States by Frank S. Meyer in the conservative magazine “National Review,” as a criticism of that establishment.
English text published by the Mises Institute

personas/adam-smith/resumen.texto: Scottish moral philosopher, professor at Glasgow and a figure of the Scottish Enlightenment. With “The Wealth of Nations” (1776) he systematized classical political economy: the division of labor, the market as an order that arises from each person's self-interest, and the critique of mercantilism.

personas/david-ricardo/resumen.texto: London stockbroker, member of Parliament and classical economist. He formulated the theory of comparative advantage, the theory of differential rent of land and a labor theory of value taken up by free traders and Marx alike.

personas/jean-baptiste-say/resumen.texto: French economist and businessman, popularizer of Adam Smith on the Continent. His “A Treatise on Political Economy” (1803) formulated the “law of markets” or “Say's law”, later summed up as “supply creates its own demand”, and highlighted the figure of the entrepreneur.

personas/john-stuart-mill/resumen.texto: English philosopher and economist, the leading liberal of his century. He wrote “Principles of Political Economy” (1848), “On Liberty” (1859) and “The Subjection of Women” (1869), and was a member of Parliament from 1865 to 1868.

personas/bastiat/resumen.texto: French economist and polemicist, free-trade activist and deputy from 1848 to 1850. With satires such as “The Candlemakers' Petition” and essays such as “The Law” and “That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen” he popularized classical liberalism and the critique of protectionism and statism.

personas/molinari/resumen.texto: Belgian economist of the French liberal school and editor of the Journal des économistes from 1881 to 1909. In “The Production of Security” (1849) he proposed that defense and justice be provided by competing private firms, an idea Rothbard considered the first formulation of anarcho-capitalism.

personas/herbert-spencer/resumen.texto: English philosopher and sociologist who applied the idea of evolution to society and coined the phrase “survival of the fittest”. He defended a minimal state in “The Man Versus the State” (1884); he is associated with social Darwinism, a label his defenders consider unfair.

personas/lysander-spooner/resumen.texto: American lawyer, abolitionist and individualist anarchist. In 1844 he founded a private mail company to compete with the federal monopoly, and in “No Treason” he denied that the Constitution binds those who did not sign it; he is a reference figure of libertarian anarchism.

personas/alberdi/resumen.texto: Jurist and writer from Tucumán, of the Generation of '37. In exile in Chile he wrote the “Bases” (1852), the main inspiration for the Constitution of 1853, and the “Sistema económico y rentístico” (1854); he championed immigration, free trade and property, and is invoked as the founder of Argentine liberalism.

personas/jevons/resumen.texto: English economist and logician at Owens College, Manchester, and University College London. With his “The Theory of Political Economy” (1871) he was, together with Menger and Walras, one of the initiators of the marginalist revolution; he also studied the depletion of British coal.

personas/walras/resumen.texto: French economist, professor at the University of Lausanne. In the “Elements of Pure Economics” (1874-1877) he formulated the first mathematical model of general equilibrium across all markets; he is one of the three initiators of the marginalist revolution.

personas/alfred-marshall/resumen.texto: English economist, professor at Cambridge and teacher of Keynes and Pigou. His “Principles of Economics” (1890) combined classical economics with marginal analysis in supply and demand curves, and was the standard textbook until the 1930s.

personas/menger/resumen.texto: Austrian economist, founder of the Austrian school. His “Principles of Economics” (1871) explained value by subjective marginal utility, and his methodological dispute with the German historical school (the Methodenstreit) gave the school its name.

personas/bohm-bawerk/resumen.texto: Austrian economist, disciple of Menger, professor at Innsbruck and Vienna and three times Austria's finance minister. He developed the theory of capital and interest (time preference and “roundabout” methods of production) and published the best-known critique of Marx's theory of value.

personas/wieser/resumen.texto: Austrian economist of the school's second generation and Böhm-Bawerk's brother-in-law. He coined the term “marginal utility” (Grenznutzen), formulated the idea of opportunity cost, succeeded Menger in his chair and was the teacher of Hayek and Schumpeter.

personas/mises/resumen.texto: Austrian economist, central figure of the school's third generation. From the Vienna Chamber of Commerce and his private seminar he argued that socialism cannot perform economic calculation; in exile in Geneva (1934) and New York (1940), he wrote “Human Action” (1949) and trained Rothbard and Kirzner.

personas/hayek/resumen.texto: Austrian-British economist and philosopher, disciple of Wieser and Mises. At the London School of Economics he debated the business cycle with Keynes; he later defended spontaneous order and dispersed knowledge against planning, founded the Mont Pelerin Society (1947) and received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1974.

personas/lionel-robbins/resumen.texto: British economist, head of the Economics department at the London School of Economics. He brought Hayek to London in 1931 as a counterweight to Keynes and defined economics as the study of the allocation of scarce means to alternative ends (1932); he later moved closer to Keynesian positions.

personas/rothbard/resumen.texto: American economist and historian, a student in Mises's seminar in New York. He combined Austrian economics with natural law and American individualist anarchism into anarcho-capitalism, and was a co-founder of the Cato Institute and a central figure of the Mises Institute.

personas/kirzner/resumen.texto: British-American economist, disciple of Mises and professor at New York University. His theory of entrepreneurship as alertness to unnoticed profit opportunities is central to the modern Austrian school; he is also a rabbi and Talmud scholar.

personas/hoppe/resumen.texto: German economist and philosopher, trained in Frankfurt under Habermas and later a disciple of Rothbard at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. He defends anarcho-capitalism with an “argumentation ethics” and argues that monarchy is preferable to democracy; his critics point to his exclusionary positions on immigration and coexistence.

personas/huerta-de-soto/resumen.texto: Spanish economist, professor of Political Economy at Rey Juan Carlos University in Madrid and the leading promoter of the Austrian school in the Spanish language. He argues that fractional-reserve banking violates property rights and causes business cycles, and proposes a 100% reserve requirement.

personas/keynes/resumen.texto: British economist at King's College, Cambridge, and the Treasury. He criticized the Treaty of Versailles, broke with the orthodoxy that expected the market to readjust on its own and argued in the “General Theory” (1936) that aggregate demand determines employment; he led the British delegation at Bretton Woods (1944).

personas/john-hicks/resumen.texto: British economist at the London School of Economics, Cambridge and Oxford. In 1937 he summarized Keynes's theory in the IS-LM model, the basis of the neoclassical synthesis, and received the Nobel Prize in 1972 with Kenneth Arrow for his work on general equilibrium and welfare.

personas/beveridge/resumen.texto: British economist and social reformer, director of the London School of Economics from 1919 to 1937. His 1942 report on social insurance was the basis of the postwar British welfare state.

personas/joan-robinson/resumen.texto: British economist at Cambridge, of Keynes's circle. She developed the theory of imperfect competition (1933), extended the “General Theory” to the long run and led, from Cambridge, the capital controversy against the MIT economists.

personas/kalecki/resumen.texto: Polish economist of Marxist training who formulated, in works from 1933 published in Polish, a theory of effective demand similar to Keynes's. He worked at Oxford and the UN and explained in 1943 why business leaders would resist permanent full employment.

personas/samuelson/resumen.texto: American economist at MIT and the first American to receive the Nobel Prize in Economics (1970). He mathematically formalized much of economic theory and spread, through his textbook “Economics”, the “neoclassical synthesis” of Keynes and price analysis.

personas/galbraith/resumen.texto: Canadian-American economist at Harvard, a Keynesian and institutionalist. He directed price controls during the Second World War, advised Kennedy and was ambassador to India; in “The Affluent Society” he criticized the power of large corporations and the contrast between private wealth and public poverty.

personas/minsky/resumen.texto: American post-Keynesian economist, professor at Washington University in St. Louis. His financial instability hypothesis holds that periods of stability encourage increasingly risky borrowing that ends in crisis; after 2008 people spoke of a “Minsky moment”.

personas/oskar-lange/resumen.texto: Polish economist, professor at Chicago and later a leader of communist Poland. In “On the Economic Theory of Socialism” (1936-1937) he answered Mises with a “market socialism” in which a central board sets prices by trial and error.

personas/schumpeter/resumen.texto: Austrian economist, student of Böhm-Bawerk and Wieser, Austria's finance minister in 1919 and professor at Harvard from 1932. He placed the innovating entrepreneur and “creative destruction” at the center of capitalist dynamics, and predicted that capitalism would give way to socialism because of its own success.

personas/polanyi/resumen.texto: Hungarian-Austrian economist, historian and anthropologist, an economic journalist in interwar Vienna and a critic of Mises. He argued in “The Great Transformation” (1944) that the self-regulating market is a recent political creation that, by treating labor, land and money as commodities, provokes a defensive reaction from society.

personas/morgenstern/resumen.texto: German-Austrian economist trained in the Austrian school, Hayek's successor as head of the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research and later a professor at Princeton. He wrote “Theory of Games and Economic Behavior” (1944) with John von Neumann.

personas/john-nash/resumen.texto: American mathematician. In his Princeton dissertation (1950) he defined the equilibrium that bears his name, the basis of non-cooperative game theory; after decades of schizophrenia he received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1994.

personas/kahneman/resumen.texto: Israeli-American psychologist. With Amos Tversky he studied the heuristics and biases with which people make decisions under uncertainty and formulated prospect theory (1979), the foundation of behavioral economics; he received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002.

personas/tversky/resumen.texto: Israeli cognitive psychologist, professor at the Hebrew University and Stanford. Together with Kahneman he documented heuristics and biases in human decision-making and formulated prospect theory; he died before their joint work received the Nobel Prize.

personas/piketty/resumen.texto: French economist at the Paris School of Economics and the EHESS. He reconstructed historical series of income and wealth from tax data and argues that, when the return on capital exceeds growth (r > g), inequality tends to increase; he proposes progressive taxes on wealth.

personas/walter-lippmann/resumen.texto: American journalist and essayist, one of the most influential political commentators of his century. His book “The Good Society” (1937), which defended a renewed liberalism, prompted the 1938 Paris colloquium that bears his name, where the term “neoliberalism” was adopted.

personas/friedman/resumen.texto: American economist, leading figure of the Chicago school and of monetarism. He argued that inflation is always a monetary phenomenon, attributed the Great Depression to the Federal Reserve's monetary contraction and defended the free market in books and on television; he received the Nobel Prize in 1976, and his 1975 visit to Pinochet and his influence on the Chicago Boys drew strong criticism.

personas/anna-schwartz/resumen.texto: American economist at the National Bureau of Economic Research. She co-authored with Milton Friedman “A Monetary History of the United States” (1963), which attributed the severity of the Great Depression to monetary contraction.

personas/stigler/resumen.texto: American economist of the Chicago school, a colleague and friend of Friedman. He studied the economics of information and the “capture” of regulators by the industries they were supposed to control, and received the Nobel Prize in 1982.

personas/coase/resumen.texto: British economist at the London School of Economics and later the University of Chicago. He explained the existence of firms by transaction costs (1937) and showed that, without those costs, the allocation of property rights does not affect efficiency (1960); he received the Nobel Prize in 1991.

personas/robert-lucas/resumen.texto: American economist at Chicago, a driving force of new classical macroeconomics. With rational expectations and the “Lucas critique” he argued that policies that exploit past statistical relationships, such as the Phillips curve, fail when people anticipate their effects; he received the Nobel Prize in 1995.

personas/arnold-harberger/resumen.texto: American economist at the University of Chicago, the main promoter of the agreement with the Catholic University of Chile (1956) that trained the “Chicago Boys”. He advised numerous Latin American governments and is known for measuring the efficiency losses caused by taxes and monopolies.

personas/buchanan/resumen.texto: American economist, founder with Gordon Tullock of public choice theory, which analyzes voters, politicians and bureaucrats as agents pursuing their own interest. He received the Nobel Prize in 1986; his work in Virginia gave its name to the “Virginia school”.

personas/tullock/resumen.texto: American economist and lawyer, co-founder with Buchanan of public choice theory. He wrote “The Calculus of Consent” (1962) with him and described “rent-seeking”: the expenditure of resources to obtain privileges from the state.

personas/hazlitt/resumen.texto: American journalist and economist, editorial writer for The New York Times and columnist for Newsweek. A friend and promoter of Mises, he wrote “Economics in One Lesson” (1946), the best-selling liberal primer, and took part in founding the FEE.

personas/leonard-read/resumen.texto: Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce executive who in 1946 founded the Foundation for Economic Education (FEE), one of the first institutions devoted to spreading economic liberalism in the United States. His essay “I, Pencil” (1958) is a popular classic on the spontaneous order of the market.

personas/john-williamson/resumen.texto: British economist at the Institute for International Economics in Washington. In 1989 he summarized in ten points the reforms that Washington-based institutions recommended to Latin America and called them the “Washington Consensus”; he later objected to the term being used as a synonym for neoliberalism.

personas/ayn-rand/resumen.texto: American novelist and philosopher, born Alisa Rosenbaum in Saint Petersburg, who emigrated in 1926. Her novels “The Fountainhead” and “Atlas Shrugged” and her Objectivist philosophy defend rational egoism and laissez-faire capitalism; she greatly influenced the libertarian movement, although she rejected it.

personas/nozick/resumen.texto: American philosopher at Harvard. In “Anarchy, State, and Utopia” (1974) he answered Rawls with a defense of the minimal state based on individual rights, which became the academic reference work of libertarianism; he later distanced himself from some of its theses.

personas/david-friedman/resumen.texto: American economist and physicist, son of Milton Friedman. He defends anarcho-capitalism on grounds of economic efficiency rather than natural rights, as Rothbard did, and has studied legal systems without a state, such as that of medieval Iceland.

personas/prebisch/resumen.texto: Economist from Tucumán, first general manager of the Banco Central de la República Argentina (1935-1943) and executive secretary of ECLAC (1950-1963). His thesis of the deterioration of the terms of trade between center and periphery founded Latin American structuralism and the policy of import substitution industrialization; he later headed UNCTAD.

personas/celso-furtado/resumen.texto: Brazilian economist at ECLAC, one of the founders of Latin American structuralism. He wrote “The Economic Growth of Brazil” (1959), headed Sudene for the development of the Northeast, and was Minister of Planning (1962-1963) and of Culture (1986-1988).
