personas/fernando-henrique-cardoso/resum.texto: Brazilian sociologist exiled in Chile after the 1964 coup, where he wrote “Dependency and Development in Latin America” with Enzo Faletto. As Finance Minister he launched the Real Plan (1994) and then served as president of Brazil (1995-2002) with stabilization and privatization policies.

personas/enzo-faletto/resumen.texto: Chilean sociologist and historian at ECLAC and the University of Chile, co-author with Cardoso of “Dependency and Development in Latin America” (1969), one of the central works of dependency theory.

personas/gunder-frank/resumen.texto: German-American economist and sociologist trained in Chicago. From Latin America he argued that underdevelopment is not an earlier stage but the result of the periphery's integration into world capitalism (“the development of underdevelopment”), the radical version of dependency theory.

personas/aldo-ferrer/resumen.texto: Argentine economist of the structuralist school. He wrote “The Argentine Economy” (1963), a widely read economic history of the country, was Minister of Economy under Levingston (1970-1971) and presided over the Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires (1983-1987).

personas/benegas-lynch-padre/resumen.texto: Argentine economist and member of the Mont Pelerin Society. Through the Centro de Difusión de la Economía Libre, which he founded in Buenos Aires in 1957 and which was later renamed Centro de Estudios sobre la Libertad, he invited Ludwig von Mises to lecture at the University of Buenos Aires in 1959.

personas/benegas-lynch-h/resumen.texto: Argentine economist, son of Alberto Benegas Lynch (father). He founded ESEADE in 1978 and for decades promoted the Austrian school and classical liberalism through books, university teaching and columns; Javier Milei acknowledges him as one of his mentors.

personas/alsogaray/resumen.texto: Argentine military engineer, politician and economist, the most visible figure of local economic liberalism in the second half of the 20th century. He was Minister of Economy under Frondizi (1959-1961) and Guido (1962), founded the UCeDé (1982) and advised the Menem government; his phrase “we must get through the winter” (1959) became an emblem of austerity plans.

hechos/revolucion-marginalista/resumen.texto: Between 1871 and 1874, Jevons in England, Menger in Austria and Walras in Switzerland independently explained value by marginal utility, that of the last available unit of a good, rather than by production cost or labor. The shift gave rise to neoclassical economics and the Austrian school.

hechos/methodenstreit/resumen.texto: Controversy between Carl Menger and Gustav Schmoller, head of the German historical school, over whether economics should build abstract theory or describe concrete historical institutions. The Germans disparagingly called Menger and his followers the “Austrian school”, and the name stuck.

hechos/creacion-de-la-reserva-federal/re.texto: The Federal Reserve Act, signed by Woodrow Wilson in December 1913, created the central bank of the United States: twelve regional banks with a board of governors in Washington. Friedman blamed it for worsening the Great Depression, and the Austrians and many libertarians call for its abolition.

hechos/debate-del-calculo-socialista/res.texto: Debate started by Mises in 1920 over whether a socialist economy can allocate resources rationally without market prices for the means of production. Oskar Lange and Abba Lerner responded with market socialism, and Hayek replied that the problem is dispersed knowledge; the Austrians saw the collapse of planned economies as confirmation of their thesis.

hechos/hiperinflacion-de-weimar/resumen.texto: To pay reparations and sustain passive resistance in the Ruhr, the German government financed its deficit by printing money, and in November 1923 one dollar was worth 4.2 trillion marks. Stabilization came with the Rentenmark, and the experience shaped German concern for monetary stability for a century.

hechos/crac-de-1929/resumen.texto: Collapse of the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929, with record falls on “Black Thursday” (the 24th) and “Black Tuesday” (the 29th), after a decade of speculation in shares bought on credit. It marked the beginning of the Great Depression.

hechos/gran-depresion/resumen.texto: Worldwide economic crisis that followed the crash of 1929: in the United States output fell by about a quarter and unemployment reached 25% in 1933, thousands of banks failed and international trade collapsed. Keynesians, monetarists and Austrians gave opposing explanations of its causes, and the experience transformed economic policy.

hechos/debate-hayek-keynes/resumen.texto: Controversy in academic journals between Hayek, of the London School of Economics, and Keynes, of Cambridge, over Keynes's “A Treatise on Money” and “Prices and Production”: Hayek attributed the crisis to prior excess credit and advised against stimulating spending, and Keynes and Piero Sraffa criticized him. The “General Theory” left Keynes the winner in his day; the debate returned to the agenda after the 2008 crisis.

hechos/new-deal/resumen.texto: Programs of Franklin D. Roosevelt's government against the Great Depression: public works, unemployment insurance and pensions (Social Security, 1935), banking and stock market regulation, support for labor unions and abandonment of the gold standard. Its supporters credit it with the recovery and the creation of a welfare state; its liberal critics, with prolonging the crisis.

hechos/coloquio-walter-lippmann/resumen.texto: Meeting of some twenty-five liberal intellectuals organized in Paris in August 1938 by Louis Rougier around Lippmann's book “The Good Society”, with Mises, Hayek, Röpke and Rüstow, among others. It discussed how to renew liberalism in the face of the crisis and collectivism, and the term “neoliberalism” was adopted there.

hechos/conferencia-de-bretton-woods/resu.texto: United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference, held in July 1944 at the Mount Washington Hotel with delegates from 44 Allied countries. Between the plan of Keynes, who proposed an international currency, and that of Harry Dexter White, for the United States, the latter prevailed: a system centered on the dollar, the IMF and the World Bank.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-fee/titulo.texto: Founding of the Foundation for Economic Education

hechos/fundacion-de-la-fee/resumen.texto: Leonard Read founded the Foundation for Economic Education in 1946 in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York, to popularize the free market, with Henry Hazlitt among its founders and Mises as a collaborator. It was the model for later libertarian think tanks.

hechos/sociedad-mont-pelerin/titulo.texto: Founding of the Mont Pelerin Society

hechos/sociedad-mont-pelerin/resumen.texto: International association of liberal economists, philosophers and historians convened by Hayek, which first met in April 1947 at Mont Pèlerin, Switzerland, with Mises, Friedman, Stigler, Popper and Robbins, among others. It became the main forum of exchange for postwar neoliberalism.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-cepal/resumen.texto: The United Nations Economic and Social Council created the Economic Commission for Latin America in February 1948, headquartered in Santiago, Chile. Under Raúl Prebisch it became the center of Latin American structuralism and the main promoter of industrialization and development planning in the region.

hechos/industrializacion-por-sustitucion.texto: Strategy followed by much of Latin America from the crisis of 1930 and theorized by ECLA after 1949: protecting local industry with tariffs and exchange controls so as to produce what had previously been imported. It achieved strong industrialization, but its critics point to the inefficiency, inflation and balance-of-payments crises it brought; it was abandoned with the reforms of the 1980s and 1990s.

hechos/mises-en-buenos-aires/resumen.texto: Invited by Alberto Benegas Lynch (father), Ludwig von Mises gave six lectures at the University of Buenos Aires in 1959 to students, professors and businesspeople, with simultaneous interpretation into Spanish. It is the milestone usually used to date the arrival of the Austrian school in Argentina.

hechos/controversia-del-capital/resumen.texto: Debate between economists from Cambridge, England, such as Joan Robinson and Piero Sraffa, and from MIT, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, such as Samuelson and Robert Solow, over whether capital can be measured as a single quantity that explains the distribution of income. Samuelson conceded his critics' objection in 1966, but neoclassical theory continued to use aggregate production functions.

hechos/premio-nobel-de-economia/titulo.texto: Creation of the Nobel Prize in Economics

hechos/premio-nobel-de-economia/resumen.texto: Sveriges Riksbank created in 1968, on its tercentenary, the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, awarded since 1969. Its recipients include Samuelson (1970), Hayek (1974, shared with Gunnar Myrdal), Friedman (1976), Buchanan (1986), Coase (1991), Lucas (1995) and Kahneman (2002); some critics object to its being presented as a Nobel Prize.

hechos/fin-de-bretton-woods/resumen.texto: On August 15, 1971, Richard Nixon suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold, imposed an import surcharge and froze prices and wages. It was the end of the Bretton Woods system: since 1973 the major currencies have floated and world money has been fiat.

hechos/fundacion-del-partido-libertario/.texto: Founding of the Libertarian Party of the United States

David Nolan and a group of activists founded the Libertarian Party in Colorado in December 1971, in reaction to Nixon's price controls, the Vietnam War and the military draft. It became the third-largest party in the United States by votes in many elections.

hechos/crisis-del-petroleo-de-1973/resum.texto: Oil embargo by the Arab exporting countries against Israel's allies in the Yom Kippur War, which quadrupled the price of crude. Together with the end of Bretton Woods it triggered “stagflation”, inflation with stagnation, which postwar Keynesian theory had not foreseen and which favored the rise of monetarism.

hechos/chicago-boys/titulo.texto: Reforms of the Chicago Boys in Chile

hechos/chicago-boys/resumen.texto: Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago through an agreement with the Catholic University (1956) ran the economic policy of Pinochet's dictatorship from 1975: trade liberalization, privatizations, reduction of the state and private pensions (1980). Their supporters speak of the “Miracle of Chile”; their critics, of a policy imposed under repression that ended in the 1982 crisis and increased inequality.

hechos/fundacion-del-instituto-cato/resu.texto: Libertarian think tank founded in 1977 by Ed Crane, Murray Rothbard and the businessman Charles Koch, based in Washington since 1981. It promotes low taxes, free markets, civil liberties and a non-interventionist foreign policy, and is one of the most influential think tanks in the United States.

hechos/thatcherismo/resumen.texto: Policy of Margaret Thatcher's government in the United Kingdom: monetary control against inflation, privatization of state enterprises, sale of public housing, financial deregulation and confrontation with the unions, as in the miners' strike of 1984-1985. Thatcher invoked Hayek and Friedman; her critics blame her for deindustrialization and rising inequality.

hechos/reaganomics/resumen.texto: Economic policy of Ronald Reagan in the United States: large tax cuts, deregulation, increased military spending and support for Paul Volcker's tight monetary policy against inflation. Inflation fell and the economy grew from 1983, but public debt nearly tripled; its critics associate it with rising inequality.

hechos/crisis-de-la-deuda-latinoamerican.texto: It began in August 1982, when Mexico declared that it could not pay its foreign debt, after a decade of loans from international banks and the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes. There followed a “lost decade” of stagnation, inflation and austerity plans negotiated with the IMF, which led to the Brady Plan and the reforms of the 1990s.

hechos/consenso-de-washington/resumen.texto: Name given by John Williamson in 1989 to ten reforms that the IMF, the World Bank and the US Treasury recommended to Latin America after the debt crisis: fiscal discipline, trade liberalization, privatizations and deregulation, among others. In the 1990s it became synonymous with the neoliberal program applied in the region, including Menem and Cavallo's Argentina; its critics hold it responsible for crises such as that of 2001.

hechos/plan-real/resumen.texto: Stabilization plan launched in Brazil in 1993 and 1994 by Finance Minister Fernando Henrique Cardoso: it created an indexed unit of account and, in July 1994, a new currency, the real, which ended decades of high inflation. Its success carried Cardoso to the presidency.

hechos/crisis-financiera-de-2008/resumen.texto: Crisis originating in US subprime mortgages and the derivatives that packaged them, which broke out with the collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 and led to the worldwide Great Recession. Governments bailed out banks and applied Keynesian-inspired stimulus; the Austrians blamed the Federal Reserve's low interest rate policy.

hechos/economia-social-de-mercado/titulo.texto: Social market economy and ordoliberalism in West Germany

hechos/economia-social-de-mercado/resume.texto: The social market economy, a term coined by Alfred Müller-Armack in 1946, combines a capitalist free-market system with social policies and the regulation necessary for fair competition. The Christian Democratic Union promoted and implemented it in West Germany from 1949, under Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, with roots in the Freiburg School and the ordoliberalism of Walter Eucken and Franz Böhm, which, unlike classical liberals, defends a strong state that guarantees competition. Ludwig Erhard, who in June 1948 had abolished price controls when the German mark was introduced, served as minister of economics for fourteen years; he saw the market itself as social and supported only a minimum of welfare legislation. The model came out of ordoliberalism but is not identical to the Freiburg School: Müller-Armack gave the state an active social role.

hechos/sistema-monetario-europeo/resumen.texto: An agreement on adjustable exchange rates among the currencies of the European Economic Community, promoted by French president Giscard d'Estaing and German chancellor Helmut Schmidt in Brussels on December 5, 1978. It took effect on March 13, 1979 with eight members and created the Exchange Rate Mechanism and the ECU unit of account. No currency was the official anchor, but in practice the German mark and the German central bank were, as the dollar was under Bretton Woods; Axel Weber argued in 1991 that it functioned as a Deutschmark zone. In September 1992 the pound and the lira left the mechanism after a wave of speculation, and in August 1993 the bands were widened from 2.25% to 15%. It lasted until 1999, when it was succeeded by economic and monetary union with the euro.

hechos/reforma-arancelaria-britanica/tit.texto: The Tariff Reform campaign in the United Kingdom

hechos/reforma-arancelaria-britanica/res.texto: Joseph Chamberlain resigned from Balfour's government in September 1903 to campaign for tariffs on imports, like those of Germany and the United States, and for imperial preference that would turn the British Empire into a trade bloc; the revenue raised would finance social reforms. The Tariff Reform League, founded in 1903, had about 250,000 members by 1914, and its Tariff Commission had the economist William Hewins as secretary. Its opponents argued that protection would make food, especially bread, more expensive. It split the Conservatives and was a factor in their defeat in 1906 by the Liberals, supporters of free trade.

hechos/debate-proteccionista-de-1875/tit.texto: Customs Law and protectionist debate of 1875

hechos/debate-proteccionista-de-1875/res.texto: To address the budget deficit and the debt from the War of the Triple Alliance, the government of Nicolás Avellaneda enacted a Customs Law in early 1875 that raised import duties on industrial products. Throughout 1875 a faction of the Autonomist current, including Dardo Rocha, Miguel Cané, Carlos Pellegrini and Vicente Fidel López, proposed in parliamentary debates some form of protectionism to industrialize the country and to stop depending on exporting primary goods and importing manufactures. Their proposals found a welcome in the press, and they were set aside as the crisis was resolved.

hechos/caja-de-conversion/titulo.texto: The Caja de Conversión and the gold standard

hechos/caja-de-conversion/resumen.texto: Law 2741 of 1890 created the Caja de Conversión (Conversion Office), the forerunner of the Central Bank, to organize note issue independently of the government; in 1895 it issued the first notes in the national peso currency and prohibited private or provincial issues. The 1890 crisis had moved the exchange rate from 1 paper peso per gold peso in 1884 to 3.87 in 1891; in 1899 it was set at 2.27 paper pesos per gold peso, and the Caja began to hand out notes only in exchange for gold. Convertibility was suspended in 1914, when World War I broke out, it was restored between 1927 and 1929, and in 1935 the Central Bank replaced it.

lugares/kings-college-cambridge/resumen.texto: College of the University of Cambridge founded by Henry VI in 1441. Keynes was a fellow from 1909 and managed its funds as bursar from 1924 until his death; he wrote the “General Theory” there.

lugares/london-school-of-economics/resum.texto: School founded in 1895 by the Fabians Sidney and Beatrice Webb, Graham Wallas and George Bernard Shaw. In the 1930s Lionel Robbins and Hayek made it the liberal pole opposite Keynes's Cambridge; it was directed by Beveridge, and Popper, Coase and Hicks taught there.

lugares/universidad-de-chicago/resumen.texto: Private university founded in 1890 with funds from John D. Rockefeller. Its Department of Economics gave its name to the Chicago school (Knight, Friedman, Stigler, Coase, Lucas), trained the Chilean “Chicago Boys” and counts many Nobel laureates in Economics. The first nuclear reactor operated beneath the stands of its stadium in 1942.

lugares/mount-washington-hotel/resumen.texto: Grand hotel in Bretton Woods, in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, opened in 1902. In July 1944 it hosted the conference that created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank and gave its name to the postwar monetary system.

lugares/mont-pelerin/resumen.texto: Village above Lake Geneva, near Vevey, in Switzerland. Its Hôtel du Parc hosted in April 1947 the founding meeting of the liberal society that bears its name.

lugares/bolsa-de-nueva-york/resumen.texto: The world's largest stock exchange, on Wall Street, born of the Buttonwood Agreement of 1792. Its collapse in October 1929 ushered in the Great Depression, and it is the symbol of American financial capitalism.

lugares/sede-de-la-cepal/resumen.texto: Headquarters of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean in Vitacura, Santiago, Chile, designed by Emilio Duhart and opened in 1966. It is a landmark of modern Latin American architecture and the place from which ECLAC developed developmentalist thought.

lugares/instituto-mises/resumen.texto: Research center founded in 1982 by Llewellyn Rockwell in Auburn, Alabama, with the support of Margit von Mises and Rothbard. It promotes the Austrian school in its Rothbardian strand and publishes most of the school's works in open access; its paleolibertarian line is disputed within liberalism itself.

lugares/universidad-francisco-marroquin/.texto: Private university in Guatemala City founded in 1971 by Manuel Ayau with an explicit orientation toward classical liberalism. It is one of the main centers for the spread of the Austrian school in Latin America, and its library is named after Ludwig von Mises.

lugares/eseade/resumen.texto: Private university institute in Buenos Aires founded in 1978 by Alberto Benegas Lynch (Jr.), devoted to graduate studies in economics and business with a classical liberal and Austrian orientation. It was one of the training centers of Argentine liberalism in the late 20th century.
